agentic_ttt.headline: RSI: Learning during the task, without losing the way
agentic_ttt.dek: Continuous test-time training inside an agent episode becomes a self-training loop. The useful question is what to learn from.
sections: Introduction

An agent can know how to solve a task and still lose it. As an episode lengthens, trajectories revisit states already explored, failed actions reappear verbatim, and strategies that worked twenty turns ago stop being sampled. The failure is not a missing capability; it is drift.

Test-time training looks like the obvious remedy: update the weights on whatever the agent just experienced. But in a multi-turn episode this is not a one-shot adaptation to a fixed prompt. Each gradient step changes the policy that generates the next batch of training text, so the agent becomes its own data source.

That loop is the object of study here. It helps while the episode keeps producing new information and it hurts once the agent is stuck generating the same text. Agentic Test-Time Training separates the two cases at token level and reports +5.0 points on ALFWorld and +4.9 on SWE-bench Lite for 1.9× the cost of not training at all.
The loop that test-time training creates

Existing LLM test-time-training methods mostly adapt once, to a fixed input. An agent episode is different: the model acts, the environment responds, the model trains on that text, and the updated model acts again. The training distribution is now a function of the parameters being trained.

This is fine while the episode is informative. It is corrosive once the agent stalls: a stuck policy emits near-identical trajectories, training on them sharpens the same wrong attractor, and the next rollout repeats it more confidently. Novelty, not volume, is what makes an update worth making.

aTTT turns that into a weighting rule. For each token in an update, the method checks whether it occurs inside an n-gram already used by a previous update; if so, its contribution to the loss is reduced, and novel tokens keep full weight. Repetition is measured against the update history of the current episode, so the filter tracks this agent’s degradation rather than a global statistic.
Three ways to decide what to learn from

What counts as experience is a separate design choice, and the paper treats the update signal as a variable: the agent’s own generated trajectory, the observations returned by the environment, or a summary of the interaction written by the model. Each has a different failure mode.

Self-generated text is the most available and the most dangerous, because it is exactly the channel through which a bad decision propagates into the weights. Environment feedback is grounded but sparse or delayed. Summaries compress a long history into something trainable but inherit the summarizer’s errors. The weighting applies to all three.

The evaluation puts that difference under pressure by contrasting immediate with delayed feedback. ALFWorld returns a household-task signal after each action; SWE-bench Lite only verifies once a patch is written and the tests run. A method that learns from repetition should behave differently in the second setting, where the same code can be retried many times before any verdict arrives.
What the gains are, and what they are not

Baselines cover the obvious alternatives: ReAct with no adaptation at all, static adaptation computed before the rollout, and unfiltered online training that updates on everything. A fourth comparison drops whole repeated updates instead of reweighting tokens inside them — the coarse version of the same idea.

Unfiltered training is the telling baseline because it isolates the cost of ignoring novelty. Dropping entire updates is the other natural remedy and is strictly blunter: an update can be partly repetitive and still contain the one new observation that matters. aTTT keeps that observation and discounts only the repeated part.

The reported improvements — up to 5.0 points on ALFWorld and 4.9 on SWE-bench Lite, averaged over three seeds — come with a caveat the authors draw themselves. Gains concentrate on tasks within the model’s existing competence. aTTT preserves a capability that long trajectories erode; on this evidence it does not teach a capability the model lacked.
Preserving competence is not recursive self-improvement

The honest framing is narrower than the RSI reading suggests. This is a bounded mechanism for keeping behaviour intact inside one episode, with per-episode LoRA adapters reset between tasks so that nothing accumulates across the benchmark.

That design choice determines the interpretation. If improvements carried across tasks, you would be looking at learning; because adapters are reset, what is measured is resistance to drift. The 1.9× overhead is the price of that resistance, and it is a serving cost as much as a training one — the runtime LoRA updates have to happen while the episode is live.

The open question is whether novelty is the right proxy. Token-level n-gram repetition is cheap and works here, but it cannot distinguish productive exploration from irrelevant variation: a genuinely new wrong turn and a genuinely new useful observation look identical to the filter. A better measure of whether an episode is still producing information would turn this from a safeguard into an adaptation signal.
keypoints: Continuous TTT in an agent episode is a self-training loop: every update changes the policy that produces the next update’s training text, so whether it helps depends on whether that text is new.
aTTT downweights the loss on tokens that appear in n-grams already used by earlier updates and leaves novel tokens fully weighted — a per-token novelty filter, not an on/off switch on whole updates.
+5.0 points on ALFWorld and +4.9 on SWE-bench Lite for 1.9× the no-TTT cost, with gains concentrated where the model already had the competence and drifted away from it.

mmg2skill.headline: RSI: From human guides to self-evolving skills
mmg2skill.dek: Web tutorials are written for people. Turning them into something an agent can execute, diagnose and revise is a separate problem.
sections: Introduction

The web is full of instructions for doing things and almost none of them were written for machines. A tutorial says drag it until it snaps, shows a screenshot instead of naming the element, and assumes you will notice when a step has failed. Hand that text to an agent and you have given it reading material, not a procedure.

The gap is not about retrieval or length, it is about form. A guide describes a goal; a skill has to be a sequence the agent can execute, check, and repair when the environment disagrees. MMG2Skill names this guide-to-skill learning and treats the conversion itself — not the final score — as the thing worth studying.

Its answer is a closed loop over an editable artifact. Guides are compiled into skills, the skills condition a fixed vision-language agent during execution, and a trajectory-level analyzer rewrites them afterwards. Across GUI control, open-ended gameplay and strategic card play with six backbones, the macro-average gain is 12.8 to 25.3 percentage points.
What a skill has to be

The design constraint is editability. If the learned artifact is a note in natural language, there is no well-defined operation for fixing the step that failed. If it is a structured procedure, a failed attempt can be traced to a specific instruction and that instruction can be changed.

This is also why the vision-language model stays frozen. Weight updates would make the improvement uninterpretable and would confound two different claims — that the agent got better, and that the procedure got better. With a fixed backbone, whatever changes is the skill text, and you can read it.

Construction is therefore a translation problem with a target format. Multimodal guides — screenshots, annotated images, surrounding prose — have to be collapsed into a procedure that refers to what the agent can actually perceive and act on. Prerequisites a human reader infers have to be made explicit, because the executor will not infer them.
Closing the loop on the agent’s own trajectories

After execution, the analyzer reads the trajectory, asks what actually went wrong, and edits the skill accordingly. The feedback is deliberately not the benchmark score: a pass/fail number cannot say which step caused the failure, and using it would tie the skill library to the evaluation set.

The same backbone is used for construction, execution, analysis and refinement. That is a control as much as a convenience — a stronger external teacher doing the analysis would make it impossible to tell whether the gains come from the loop or from the teacher.

MMG2Skill-Bench supplies the testbed across GUI tasks, gameplay and strategic card play, the last of which adds private information the agent cannot observe. That setting is analysed separately, and for a reason: if the decisive information is hidden, no amount of trajectory analysis can recover the true cause of a failure.
Where the gains come from

Main results compare three conditions — no skills, raw guides, and the full loop — averaged over six backbones with five attempts allowed and the analyzer’s early-stop decision in force. Every model-domain setting improves, with macro-average gains between 12.8 and 25.3 points.

The most informative ablation is the one that fails. Prompting with raw guides can reduce performance: unstructured instructions add noise and misleading detail, and the agent has no way to tell which part of a tutorial applies to the state it is in. Structure is doing real work, not re-tokenising the same content.

Removing revision removes the rest of the gain, which separates the two contributions cleanly. Early stopping is a third and separate effect: when the success signal is calibrated, the analyzer can stop before the attempt budget is spent, saving 25%–53% of attempts and avoiding the late-stage regressions that come from continuing to edit an already-correct skill.
An improvement you can read, and one that can be misled

Because nothing is written into the weights, this is self-improvement in a form you can audit. Given a failing run you can point to the instruction that changed and to the trajectory that caused the change. For deployment, that traceability is often worth more than the raw score.

The corresponding weakness is calibration. An analyzer that declares success too early will preserve a skill that happened to work once, and the procedure stops evolving. The paper’s caveat is precise: early stopping helps when the success signal is properly calibrated, which is a property of the environment rather than of the method.

That is the boundary to carry away. Where the outcome is observable from the trajectory, the loop closes and the skill library compounds. Where decisive information is hidden — a card the agent cannot see, a server state it cannot query — root-cause analysis is guessing, and the honest expectation is no gain rather than a smaller one.
keypoints: A guide is not a skill: tutorials assume a human executor, mix text with images and leave recovery steps implicit. The framework compiles them into an editable procedure instead of prompting with the raw text.
Revision is driven by trajectory-level root-cause analysis, never by benchmark scores, and the vision-language model is never updated — everything learned lives in the skill library.

Raw guides can actively hurt. Prompting with the unprocessed guide degrades performance, while structured construction and trajectory-driven revision are each necessary for the +12.8 to +25.3 point macro-average gains.

webcompass.headline: Evaluating the whole web-coding workflow
webcompass.dek: A page can be valid code and still be unusable. WebCompass scores generation, editing and repair by running the result in a browser.
sections: Introduction

A generated page can be syntactically valid, pass every static check, and still be unusable: the layout collapses at another viewport, the button does nothing, the form silently discards input. Static correctness metrics were never designed to see any of that.

Web engineering is also not a single act. A site is generated, then changed, then repaired, and most of the real cost sits in the second and third. Benchmarks that score only one-shot text-to-code generation measure the easiest part of the job and report it as the whole.

WebCompass is built around that gap. It spans three input modalities — text, image, video — and three task types — generation, editing, repair — giving seven categories, and it judges generation by actually driving the site in a browser instead of reading its source.
Generation, editing, repair

The three task types are not three difficulties of the same skill. Generation asks whether something works at all. Editing asks whether a requested change lands without breaking everything the request did not mention. Repair asks whether a specific defect is fixed without losing interactions that already worked.

That last clause is where most repairs fail. A fix can remove the bug and take the hover state, the keyboard path and the error message with it. Scoring repair only on whether the defect is gone would reward exactly that trade.

Editing and repair are judged with checklist-guided evaluation, which is the right tool when the intended change is known in advance: the checklist states what must hold, and the judge checks each item instead of forming a global impression. Generation has no such list, which is why it needs a different mechanism.
Executing the page instead of reading it

For generation, WebCompass uses an agent as the judge. It loads the produced site in a real browser, navigates it, triggers interactions through Chrome DevTools MCP, and iteratively writes test cases against what it finds. The result resembles a QA engineer’s acceptance run more than a code review.

This matters because a screenshot is a state, not a behaviour. Two screenshots can look identical while one belongs to a page whose filter works and the other to a page whose filter silently does nothing. Only execution separates them.

The evaluation keeps three dimensions separate — can the site run, does it meet the requirement, does it look right — and averages nine scores overall. Ten multimodal models are tested through Claude Code 2.0.67, with further analyses on difficulty, framework and thinking mode.
What the results actually show

Closed-source models are stronger and, more tellingly, more balanced. Open-source entries tend to show a sharp profile, with one or two dimensions carrying the score while the others lag — a shape that a single aggregate number would flatten into an average.

Aesthetics is the persistent bottleneck and it is not close. Models that produce functioning applications still produce plainly unattractive ones, and the gap is widest for open-source models — a reminder that visual quality is a separate capability from code correctness, not a cosmetic add-on to it.

Two secondary findings are easy to lose in a ranking. Editing and repair have distinct difficulty profiles: repair tends to preserve interactivity better but remains harder to execute. And framework choice materially moves the score, with Vue consistently challenging and React or Vanilla/HTML stronger depending on the task — so part of a model’s web-coding score is really a fact about its default stack.
Reading a benchmark as a profile

The practical instruction is to stop treating web coding as one number. Runability, requirement adherence and visual quality fail independently, and a model can be excellent at two and unacceptable at the third.

The benchmark’s own limits should travel with its scores. Judges are automated, so dimension-level results inherit the judge’s blind spots, and a real browser runtime ties the measurement to one environment. A single aggregate ranking compresses both away.

The larger point is about what working means for generated software. Correct code is a precondition, not a deliverable. If evaluation only checks the precondition, training will optimise for it, and the thing users actually judge — whether the product works and looks right — stays unmeasured.
keypoints: Seven task categories from three input modalities × three task types, covering 15 generation domains, 16 editing operation types and 11 repair defect types, each graded Easy / Medium / Hard.

Generation is scored by an Agent-as-a-Judge that launches the site in a real browser, explores interactions through Chrome DevTools MCP and writes targeted test cases — acceptance testing rather than code review.

Across ten multimodal models, closed-source stays stronger and more balanced; aesthetics is the most persistent bottleneck, especially for open-source; and framework choice materially moves the score, with Vue consistently hard.

color.headline: Aligning generative detail with image structure
color.dek: The failure is spectral: isotropic objectives cannot tell an authentic high-frequency detail from a hallucinated one.
sections: Introduction

Generative super-resolution is very good at producing detail and not very good at producing detail that belongs to the input. Given a blurred patch it will invent a plausible window frame, a plausible eyelash, a plausible texture — and a perceptual metric will reward it for doing so.

The paper’s diagnosis is geometric rather than architectural. Natural images distribute information unevenly across frequency: most of the energy sits in a thin low-frequency band, while high frequencies carry the structure and very little of the energy. An objective built on isotropic Gaussian noise treats every direction in image space as equally important, which is precisely wrong for that distribution.

ASASR rebuilds the alignment objective in the geometry the image distribution actually has. The noise transition kernel is coloured to follow natural spectral decay, placing the generative flow in a Sobolev-induced Riemannian metric, and a learned adversary supplies the negative examples. In a study with 50 participants over 64 images it is preferred 91.1% of the time on naturalness and fidelity.
Sobolev geometry, and an adversary that finds the worst direction

Preference optimisation needs a negative example — something to prefer the correct reconstruction over. The standard choice is a sample from the same spectrally flat Gaussian noise used to train the model, and ASASR’s first move is to replace it with noise whose spectrum follows the natural decay of real images.

Concretely, this recasts the generative flow in a Sobolev-induced Riemannian geometry. Distance is no longer measured in flat L2 but with frequency-dependent weights, so a change in a band where natural images carry structure counts for more than an equally large change in a band that carries mostly noise.

The second piece supplies the negatives. Rather than sampling random failures, a parametric adversary grounded in the Riesz representation theorem synthesises examples equivalent to worst-case Sobolev gradients: it searches for the direction in which the current output most violates structure, and alignment is trained against that instead of against noise.
Why geometry rather than a stronger penalty

It is fair to ask why this is not simply a reweighted loss. The difference is where the weighting lives. A penalty applied on top of an isotropic objective still compares two images in a space where all directions are equal; changing the geometry changes the space in which the comparison takes place.

This matters because the failure mode is asymmetric. Adding a high-frequency detail that is not there and failing to reconstruct one that is may cost the same in L2, but they are not equivalent errors — one is invention, the other is loss. A metric aligned with the image spectrum separates them.

The adversary is what makes the objective adversarial rather than merely weighted. Random negatives mostly produce easy examples, perturbations the model already handles, so training against them spends capacity where it buys nothing. Worst-case gradients concentrate the signal on the structural failures that actually occur.
Measuring structure, not just preference

Perceptual scores alone cannot establish fidelity, because they are exactly the quantity a generative model can optimise without being faithful. The evaluation therefore asks three separate questions: does the image look natural, does its frequency content match the reference, and does useful semantic content survive restoration.

The second and third questions are the load-bearing ones. Spectral comparison tests the paper’s actual claim about frequency structure, while downstream detection, segmentation and OCR test whether restored detail still carries information a machine can use — a stricter requirement than looking right to a human.

Ablations isolate the two contributions by replacing Sobolev guidance with Euclidean guidance and by removing adversarial alignment. That design matters because both components could plausibly improve appearance; only the spectral and downstream measurements can say whether they improved fidelity.
Fidelity is not sharpness

The headline result is a 91.1% first-choice rate for naturalness and fidelity in a study with 50 participants and 64 test images, alongside improved spectral consistency and downstream task performance. Read together they support one specific claim: alignment in a frequency-aware geometry preserves structure that an isotropic objective loses.

The scope is narrower than a general fidelity guarantee. The results hold under the paper’s degradation model and evaluation settings, and a user study of this size establishes preference rather than correctness — participants judge plausibility, and plausibility is the thing generative models fake best.

What transfers is the objective-design lesson. If a generative prior is aligned in a metric that ignores the spectrum of the data, it will be rewarded for inventing detail. Making the metric reflect the data distribution is a cheap change with a measurable consequence, and the downstream tasks are the check that keeps it honest.
keypoints: The diagnosis is spectral, not architectural. Isotropic objectives and spectrally flat Gaussian noise weight all frequencies equally, so they cannot distinguish a real high-frequency detail from an invented one.

ASASR colours the noise transition kernel to mirror natural spectral decay, recasting the generative flow in a Sobolev-induced geometry, and adds an adversary whose negatives are worst-case Sobolev gradients rather than random samples.
91.1% first-choice rate in a 50-participant study over 64 images, with spectral comparisons and downstream detection, segmentation and OCR as structural checks instead of perceptual scores alone.

tta_flow.headline: Using inference-time feedback for image restoration
tta_flow.dek: ResFlow-Tuner separates conditioning from steering: one is architectural, the other is a compute budget you can dial.
sections: Introduction

A text-to-image diffusion model contains an enormous amount of knowledge about what images look like. Using one for restoration means overriding that knowledge with a specific damaged input: the prior must generate, but it must generate this photograph.

Two problems have to be solved and they are usually conflated. The model has to receive the degraded image and any semantic context in a form it can condition on, and it has to be steered toward a reconstruction rather than toward a generic plausible image. The first is architectural; the second is an inference-time question.

ResFlow-Tuner, built on FLUX.1-dev, keeps them apart. Unified multimodal fusion handles conditioning, and a training-free test-time scaling procedure uses reward feedback to adjust the denoising direction during inference. On LSDIR-Val the scaling step alone moves LPIPS from 0.4015 to 0.3721 and FID from 22.91 to 19.82.
Conditioning the prior, then steering it

FLUX.1-dev is a multi-modal diffusion transformer: text and image tokens already live in one sequence. Unified multimodal fusion exploits that by encoding the degraded image and the semantic condition into the same shared sequence, so the transformer attends across both rather than receiving the image through a side adapter.

Why it matters: an adapter path forces the condition to compete with the model’s own prior at a fixed strength. Putting the condition inside the sequence lets attention decide, at every layer, how much the degraded observation should constrain generation.

The second half happens at inference and needs no training. A reward model scores intermediate candidates and that signal adjusts the denoising direction. Nothing about FLUX changes; what changes is how much computation is spent searching among trajectories the model already supports.
Spending compute where it pays

Test-time scaling reframes restoration as an allocation problem. Each input receives a budget, and the budget buys additional candidate trajectories that are scored and pruned instead of a single uncontrolled sample.

That is a different trade from training a larger model. Training cost is paid once and applies to every input; test-time compute is paid per input, so it can be spent unevenly — heavily on a difficult photograph, barely on an easy one — which is the right shape for a restoration service with a long tail.

The ablations therefore separate the design choices rather than reporting only a final configuration: how the low-quality image and text are fused, which reward signals steer the process, and how much compute is spent. Varying the budget is the part that matters most for anyone deciding whether to adopt it.
What the scaling buys

On LSDIR-Val, going from no test-time scaling to K=4 and N=7 improves LPIPS from 0.4015 to 0.3721 and FID from 22.91 to 19.82, with MUSIQ rising from 71.47 to 74.21. LPIPS and FID moving together is the informative part: the output is closer to the reference and drawn from a distribution closer to real images.

These gains are not free, and the paper reports the price rather than hiding it. The improvement is bought with additional sampling and reward evaluations per input; the method is tunable, which is the point rather than a caveat.

OCR evaluation is the check that keeps the numbers honest. Text is where the difference between sharper and more correct is observable: a reconstruction can render crisper glyphs that read as different characters. If OCR accuracy improves alongside LPIPS, the detail being added is real rather than decorative.
A dial, not a promise

The useful reading is that inference compute becomes a controllable parameter of a restoration system. A batch pipeline can spend a large budget and an interactive one can spend almost none, using the same weights.

The limitation sits in the reward model. Steering optimises whatever the reward can measure, so a reward that favours sharpness will trade fidelity for sharpness exactly as a hand-designed loss would. The reward choice is not a neutral implementation detail; it is where the method’s values are set.

That is why the ablations matter more than the headline. They support a tunable method whose quality depends on the reward and the budget, not an unconditional claim that more inference always yields a better reconstruction. Anyone deploying it should re-measure the reward’s behaviour on their own degradation distribution.
keypoints: Conditioning and steering are separated: unified multimodal fusion places the low-quality image and text in one sequence for the MM-DiT, while a training-free test-time scaling step steers denoising with reward-model feedback.
The budget is a dial, not a setting: with K=4 and N=7 on LSDIR-Val, LPIPS falls from 0.4015 to 0.3721, FID from 22.91 to 19.82 and MUSIQ rises from 71.47 to 74.21.
Because nothing is retrained, the same weights serve a latency-sensitive and a quality-sensitive path — the trade is per-input compute instead of one committed model.

shiftlut.headline: A wider view for efficient image restoration
shiftlut.dek: Expanding a look-up table’s receptive field usually costs storage and latency. Moving the context instead of the table costs almost nothing.
sections: Introduction

A look-up table is one of the cheapest ways to do image restoration: precompute the mapping from a local patch to an output value, then index it at inference. The reason it is cheap is also its limitation — a pointwise table sees almost no spatial context.

The obvious remedy is a bigger table indexed by a bigger neighbourhood, and that is where the cost explodes. Entries grow combinatorially with the number of input pixels used, so storage and latency climb together, and the last few years of LUT work have largely been trading efficiency for receptive field.

ShiftLUT goes at all three costs at once and reports the largest receptive field among LUT methods — 3.8× that of TinyLUT — while improving average PSNR by more than 0.21 dB and reducing both storage and runtime in the reported configuration.
Moving context instead of enlarging tables

The first component is a learnable spatial shift. Rather than index a table with a larger patch, the network shifts feature channels by learnable offsets before the lookup, so different channels carry information from different positions and the effective receptive field grows without the table growing.

This is a reallocation rather than an addition. A shift costs almost nothing — it is an index manipulation, not a convolution — so the context is paid for in memory layout rather than in multiply-accumulates. Per-channel offsets let the network decide how far each channel should look.

The second component accepts that the two branches do not carry equal information. An asymmetric dual-branch architecture gives more computation to the information-dense branch instead of splitting capacity evenly, which lowers latency without the quality drop a symmetric cut would cause.
Storage is a budget too

The third component addresses a cost that FLOP counts hide. On an edge device the table itself has to live in memory, and error-bounded adaptive sampling compresses it by sampling the table non-uniformly with a bound on the resulting interpolation error.

The bound is the point. Downsampling a LUT uniformly is easy but degrades outputs unpredictably; sampling adaptively under an error bound turns compression into a controlled trade between storage and maximum error rather than a guess.

Treating storage, latency and quality as one budget is what separates this from a PSNR paper. The small, medium and large variants exist so that a deployment can choose a point on that surface instead of inheriting the researcher’s.
Reading the measurements

Evaluation covers 4× super-resolution, denoising and JPEG deblocking, with PSNR and SSIM on the luminance channel across standard SR datasets, plus a runtime measurement from an Android implementation on a Snapdragon 888 at 320×180 input.

The three tasks matter because receptive field is not equally valuable in each. Deblocking is largely a local operation, while super-resolution benefits most from wider context. Removing the final spatial enlargement stage and still seeing gains is the evidence that the mechanism is not specific to upscaling.

The comparison worth keeping in view is Manga109: 29.16 dB against TinyLUT-F’s 28.83 dB, with storage down from 171 KB to 104 KB and runtime down from 146 ms to 84 ms. Better quality with less memory and less time at once is the unusual part — normally you buy one with another.
Deployment defines the claim

The model family is the contribution. A single best score would tell a deployer nothing, whereas a storage–quality–latency surface with three variants lets one pick a configuration for a specific device and input size.

The efficiency claim is scoped by how it was measured. Phone model, input resolution and degradation model all move runtime, and 320×180 is a small frame — the same ratios need not hold at 1080p, where memory traffic behaves differently.

What transfers is the design argument. When a cheap operator is cheap because it sees too little, adding context can be cheaper than enlarging the operator. That reframing is worth more than the 0.21 dB and applies wherever a pointwise module is being stretched to do a spatial job.
keypoints: Context without a bigger table: a learnable spatial shift applies channel-wise offsets to the feature map, so information from other positions reaches each channel before the lookup instead of being indexed by a larger neighbourhood.

An asymmetric two-branch architecture gives more computation to the information-dense branch, and error-bounded adaptive sampling compresses feature-level tables with a bound on interpolation error — storage, not just FLOPs, is treated as a budget.
On Manga109, ShiftLUT-L reaches 29.16 dB against TinyLUT-F at 28.83 dB, with reported storage falling from 171 KB to 104 KB and runtime from 146 ms to 84 ms on a Snapdragon 888 at 320×180.

instantvir.headline: Bringing diffusion-based video restoration to real time
instantvir.dek: Distillation moves iterative sampling out of serving and into training — a causal student learns to hit a bidirectional teacher’s target in one pass.
sections: Introduction

Restoring a video stream is an inverse problem with a deadline. You observe a degraded sequence and want the clean one, but the answer has to arrive before the next frames do — which rules out the methods that currently produce the best reconstructions.

The two available options fail in specific ways. Adapting an image diffusion model frame by frame and adding a temporal regulariser produces flicker, because consistency is imposed after the fact rather than modelled. Using a native video diffusion model properly needs iterative posterior sampling, which is orders of magnitude too slow for streaming.

InstantViR removes the iteration by moving it into training. A bidirectional video diffusion teacher is distilled into a causal autoregressive student that maps a degraded clip to a restored one in a single forward pass, reporting 35.56 FPS for the LeanVAE variant and up to 100× speedups over iterative solvers.
Distilling iteration into a single pass

Teacher and student face different constraints. The teacher can look at the whole clip and use future frames when reconstructing the present; the student, running on a stream, cannot. Distillation transfers the teacher’s reconstruction behaviour into a form that respects that causality.

The student is autoregressive over time, so each frame is produced from what has already arrived, while the training target comes from a model that had the luxury of bidirectional context. This is the standard reason to distill: the expensive model sets the target and the cheap model learns to hit it.

LeanVAE addresses the cost that remains once iteration is gone. Even a single pass through a video diffusion model spends much of its time encoding and decoding latents, so replacing the backbone VAE with a lighter one — through teacher-space regularised distillation — is where a further roughly 2.5× of throughput comes from.
Supervision from the forward operator

Amortised restoration usually needs pairs: a clean video and its degraded version, collected or synthesised. InstantViR avoids them by using known degradation operators instead — inpainting masks, blur kernels, downsampling — which can be applied to any candidate clean video to produce the measurement it should have yielded.

That turns training into a consistency requirement. The student proposes a clean clip, the known forward operator predicts what the sensor would have recorded, and the discrepancy is the training signal. No external paired data is needed and the inverse problem stays explicit rather than being folded into a learned prior.

The trade is scope. Known operators cover degradations you can write down, which is most of what capture and streaming pipelines produce. Degradations that are not modelled — an unknown sensor pipeline, codec artifacts — lie outside what the student was trained to invert.
Throughput, and what it depends on

Training uses 6,000 Open-Sora clips with measurements generated through known forward operators; evaluation uses 500 held-out clips plus REDS30 for zero-shot transfer, covering random inpainting, Gaussian deblurring and 4× super-resolution at 832×480.

The paper measures per-frame fidelity, perceptual quality, temporal distribution and throughput, and reports the original-VAE model separately from the LeanVAE variant — 13.91 and 35.56 FPS on a single NVIDIA A800 80GB. Reporting both is what makes the number usable.

Across the three tasks the one-step approach matches or surpasses diffusion baselines on the reported temporal and reconstruction measures. That is the substantive result: the speedup is not bought with a large quality drop, because the student inherits the teacher’s prior rather than approximating it from scratch.
Real time is a property of a setup

Distillation moves iterative work from serving time into training time. That is the right trade when many clips share a known restoration task, and a worse one when the degradation changes often or when inputs fall outside the training distribution.

The throughput figure also needs its conditions attached. Model variant, resolution and hardware all move it, and 832×480 on one accelerator is a specific operating point — quoting frames per second without those is why real-time claims are so hard to compare across papers.

The interesting consequence is what becomes possible rather than what gets faster. At tens of frames per second, diffusion-quality restoration fits into interactive and editable streaming pipelines — telepresence, AR/VR, live capture — where an iterative solver was never a candidate regardless of its quality.
keypoints: Distillation rather than approximation: a bidirectional video diffusion teacher is distilled into a causal autoregressive student that restores in one forward pass, inheriting temporal modelling while removing iterative test-time optimisation.

The distillation is prior-driven — it needs only the teacher and known degradation operators, with no externally paired clean/degraded video dataset. A forward model connects a candidate clean clip to the measurement it would have produced.

35.56 FPS for the LeanVAE variant and 13.91 FPS for the original-VAE model, measured on a single NVIDIA A800 80GB, with up to 100× speedups over iterative video diffusion solvers across inpainting, deblurring and super-resolution.

varsr.headline: Restoring images one scale at a time
varsr.dek: Super-resolution has a correct coarse answer already: the input. Next-scale prediction builds on it instead of inventing one.
sections: Introduction

Autoregression is how language models work: predict the next token conditional on everything before it. Images have no obvious token order, which is one reason diffusion dominated generation — until next-scale prediction reframed the sequence as coarse-to-fine rather than left-to-right.

Super-resolution fits that framing better than text-to-image does. There is already a correct low-resolution answer, namely the input, so the problem is not inventing an image but deciding what detail to add on top of one that is given.

VARSR builds on this with next-scale prediction, conditioning every scale on prefix tokens derived from the low-resolution image, and adds scale-aligned rotary positional encodings plus a diffusion refiner for quantization residuals. In a 50-image study it is selected 55.2% of the time among six methods, at roughly a tenth of DiffBIR’s reported runtime.
Coarse first, then detail

Next-scale prediction does not order pixels spatially. The model predicts a coarse token map, then a finer one conditioned on it, then a finer one still, so each level is generated knowing what the level above has already committed to.

The ordering is a strong structural prior. A spatially autoregressive model can produce a plausible left half and a plausible right half that disagree at the seam; a coarse-to-fine model cannot, because global layout is decided at the scale where it is cheapest to decide.

The low-resolution input enters as prefix tokens — a sequence the autoregressive model attends to at every scale rather than a conditioning vector injected once. That targets a specific failure mode: generative super-resolution drifting from the input because the condition was applied only at the first step.
Making scales comparable

Two problems follow from predicting at several resolutions. Positions at different scales do not correspond under a naive positional encoding, and a discrete tokenizer cannot represent the continuous residual between its quantization and the true pixel values.

Scale-aligned rotary positional encoding fixes the first by rescaling positions so that the same image location keeps a consistent relative position across scales. Without it the model has to relearn the correspondence at every level, which wastes capacity on something that could be built in.

The diffusion refiner fixes the second by modelling the quantization residual so that the final output reaches pixel-level fidelity. The split matters for credit assignment: the autoregressive model owns semantic structure, and the refiner owns only what discretization threw away.
What next-scale prediction delivers

The evaluation combines reference-based metrics, no-reference quality scores, visual comparison and human preference. That combination is the right one here, because a method can win on perceptual scores while losing on fidelity and any single one of those numbers would hide it.

The 55.2% selection rate in a 50-image study across six methods is the preference result, and 0.59 s per image is the efficiency one. The ablations that carry the argument are the ones comparing prefix-token conditioning against alternative ways of injecting the low-resolution image.

Those ablations exist to answer a fair objection. A diffusion refiner can produce impressive detail on its own, so a strong result might come from the refiner rather than from autoregressive restoration. Separating the positional encoding and the refiner is what makes this a claim about next-scale prediction instead of about the pipeline.
Representation, not just architecture

The transferable idea is to choose the representation before choosing the network. Coarse structure is decided where it is cheap, fine detail is conditioned on it, and the input remains an explicit condition throughout — a principle that does not depend on this particular tokenizer.

The caveat is the one that applies to every generative restoration method. Realism and fidelity are in tension, and a model that wins a preference study may still add texture that was not in the scene. Prefix-token conditioning reduces drift; it does not certify the absence of hallucination.

The efficiency comparison should also be read with its assumptions intact — hardware, image size and implementation all move it, so 10.1% of DiffBIR’s runtime is a statement about one measurement setup. The interesting claim is that autoregression can be cheaper here, because the coarse levels are cheap to predict.
keypoints: Super-resolution is cast as next-scale prediction: a coarse representation is established first and successive scales are predicted from it, with the low-resolution image entering as prefix tokens rather than as a one-shot condition.

Scale-aligned rotary positional encodings keep locations comparable across resolutions, and a diffusion refiner models the quantization residual — separating semantic structure from what a discrete tokenizer cannot represent.
55.2% of selections in a 50-image user study on DRealSR and RealSR across six methods, at 0.59 s per image — about 10.1% of DiffBIR’s reported runtime in the same setup.

tinvblocks.headline: Rethinking the information kept in a smaller image
tinvblocks.dek: Learned rescaling controls both directions, so the low-resolution image is a designed container. What goes in it is the design decision.
sections: Introduction

Image rescaling is not super-resolution with extra steps. Downscaling and upscaling are designed together, so the low-resolution image is not an arbitrary degraded input but a container the system itself filled — and what it chose to put there determines what can later be recovered.

Invertible networks make this explicit. One network handles both directions: a forward map that must be invertible by construction, plus a learned distribution for whatever is discarded. The usual design splits the representation into a low-frequency branch and a high-frequency branch, models the high-frequency part as noise, and processes the low-frequency part directly in RGB.

T-InvBlocks changes what the surviving branch holds. It separates luminance from chrominance so the invertible map stops spending capacity on the correlation between R, G and B, and it forces the high-frequency input to zero at reconstruction time. Inserted into existing pipelines it gains 0.4–0.6 dB at 2× under JPEG compression at comparable parameter counts.
Three branches, three jobs

A vanilla invertible block splits its input in two and couples the halves with affine transforms that are invertible by construction. One half becomes the low-frequency representation that survives as the small image; the other is the high-frequency detail that must be stored or sampled at reconstruction time.

The tri-branch version is not a third prediction of the same image. It divides the surviving half into luminance and chrominance and keeps the high-frequency branch as a third path, so each branch has a distinct role in the mapping rather than three copies of one job.

The all-zero high-frequency mapping is the sharpest choice. At upscaling time the detail branch is fed zeros instead of a sampled code, which removes the option of leaning on generated detail and pressures the learned downscaler to keep whatever will actually be needed inside the small image.
Why RGB is the wrong space for the surviving half

The redundancy argument is concrete. In a natural image the three RGB channels are strongly correlated — much of what the R channel says is predictable from G and B — so a block processing them jointly spends capacity transmitting essentially the same luminance structure three times.

Splitting into Y and CbCr concentrates most of the perceptually relevant information in one channel and leaves two low-bandwidth chrominance channels. The invertible coupling then operates on a representation whose channels mean different things instead of on three near-copies.

This is why the gain comes from redesigning what is stored rather than from adding depth. The block reportedly drops into existing architectures at comparable parameter counts, which is the signature of a representation change and not of a capacity increase.
What changes when the branches change

The evaluation inserts the block into two different families — IRN-style rescaling and SAIN-style compression-aware pipelines — and tests ordinary reconstruction alongside JPEG-compressed reconstruction across several quality factors and 2×/4× scaling.

Testing across two hosts is the load-bearing part. A gain that appears in only one complete network could come from an interaction with that network; the same block improving two architectures points at the representation rather than at the host.

The JPEG setting is the honest test of the idea. Lossy encoding will discard part of the small image regardless, so the real question is whether information was placed where the codec is likely to keep it. Gains of 0.4–0.6 dB at 2× and 0.2–0.5 dB at 4× suggest it was.
Rescaling as information allocation

The framing that generalises is allocation. Because encoder and decoder are trained together, the system decides what the small image carries; once that is a design variable, luminance/chrominance separation and zero-detail reconstruction are both ways of spending the budget better.

The scope is narrower than super-resolution. This assumes a coordinated encode/decode pipeline where the downscaler is yours. Recovering an arbitrary image from the web is a different problem with none of this control, and the numbers should not be read as a claim about that setting.

One practical limit is worth naming. Forcing recovery information into the small image means that image carries structure a codec may treat as noise. Robustness under JPEG is evidence it works at the tested quality factors, not a guarantee across every compression pipeline a deployment might use.
keypoints: Learned rescaling controls both sides of the compression: the low-resolution image is a designed representation, not an arbitrary degraded input, so where information is placed is part of the model.

The low-frequency branch is split into luminance (Y) and chrominance (CbCr) instead of RGB, removing channel redundancy, and reconstruction uses an all-zero high-frequency input so recovery information has to live in the small image.

Plug-and-play: inserted into IRN-style rescaling and SAIN-style compression-aware pipelines, T-SAIN gains 0.4–0.6 dB at 2× and 0.2–0.5 dB at 4× over SAIN on JPEG-compressed DIV2K, at comparable parameter counts.

oapt.headline: Restoring images after a second JPEG compression
oapt.dek: Two JPEG passes with different block grids put up to four artifact patterns inside one 8×8 block. The offset between the grids is the missing information.
sections: Introduction

A photograph is usually compressed more than once. It is saved by a camera, cropped or edited, then saved again and uploaded, and each JPEG pass lays its own 8×8 block grid over the image. Nothing guarantees those grids line up.

When they do not, the artifact structure stops being uniform. The paper’s analysis counts up to four distinct artifact patterns inside a single 8×8 block, because a block of the second compression can straddle four blocks of the first, each with its own quantization history.

That observation is the whole method. Rather than treat double compression as harder single compression, OAPT estimates the offset between the two grids and groups pixels by the pattern they belong to, gaining more than 0.16 dB over the compared state of the art.
Four patterns in one block

JPEG splits an image into 8×8 blocks, applies a discrete cosine transform to each, then quantizes the coefficients. Quantization is what loses information, and it is applied per block, so the artifact pattern a pixel shows is determined by which grid cell it fell into.

Apply the grid twice with a crop or shift in between and the second grid no longer coincides with the first. A block in the second pass can overlap four blocks from the first, each quantized independently, so four different artifact signatures coexist inside one block.

This is why models trained for single compression degrade. Their implicit assumption is that artifact structure is spatially uniform at the block scale, and that is exactly what a second misaligned pass breaks. Restoration requires knowing which pattern each pixel belongs to.
Grouping by compression history

OAPT’s first module predicts the offset between the two compression grids. With the offset known, pixels inside any window can be partitioned by which block of the first compression they came from — that is, by their compression history rather than by their coordinates.

The reconstruction network then uses hybrid partition attention blocks. Window-based self-attention handles ordinary local structure, while a sparse attention branch operates over the clustered pattern features, connecting positions that share an artifact signature however far apart they sit.

The two are genuinely complementary. Window attention is good at neighbourhoods and blind to the fact that two pixels on opposite sides of a block boundary may share a quantization history; sparse pattern attention captures exactly that and is useless for local texture.
What offset-aware grouping recovers

Training synthesises the degradation rather than collecting it: JPEG, then a pixel shift, then JPEG again, with both quality factors sampled from 5 to 95 and offsets from zero to seven pixels. One model covers the whole range instead of one model per setting.

That choice matters for the claim. Sampling both quality factors broadly forces the offset predictor to work both when the first compression was nearly lossless and when it was severe, which is the range real editing histories actually produce.

The reported gain over the compared state of the art exceeds 0.16 dB on double-JPEG restoration, and the pattern-clustering component transfers: inserted into other transformer restoration models it improves them without extra computation. That transfer is the strongest evidence the clustering captures something real about the degradation rather than fitting this network.
Degradation structure belongs in the architecture

The generalisable move is to expose the structure of the degradation to the attention mechanism. Pixels that look unrelated spatially can share a compression history, and once grouping reflects that, the model can learn relationships it otherwise could not.

The method is also correctly narrow. It models double JPEG specifically — two compression passes with one shift between them. Predictions are only as good as the offset estimator, and a history involving resizing, another codec or more passes introduces structure the model never saw.

For deployment that is a scoping question rather than a defect. Real pipelines have known, enumerable degradation histories, and the useful contribution is a method that turns one specific history into an architectural prior — at the cost of not generalising beyond it.
keypoints: A block of the second JPEG can straddle up to four blocks of the first, so a single 8×8 block may contain as many as four distinct artifact patterns — the degradation is piecewise, not uniform.

A compression offset predictor estimates the shift between the two grids; those estimates partition the features, and hybrid partition attention blocks combine window self-attention with sparse attention over the grouped features.

The pattern-clustering module is a plugin: it can be inserted into other transformer-based restoration models without added computation, and the gain over the compared state of the art exceeds 0.16 dB.

cpga.headline: Recovering video detail from the codec’s own clues
cpga.dek: An encoder already estimated motion and recorded what its prediction missed. CPGA feeds both back into the enhancer.
sections: Introduction

A compressed video carries more than the pixels you decode. To build a bitstream the encoder already estimated how content moves between frames and recorded what its prediction could not explain. Motion vectors and residuals are two byproducts most enhancement methods simply throw away.

They are not redundant with the decoded frames. A motion vector is a compact statement about where information is expected to move; a residual marks where the codec’s prediction failed, which is usually where detail is densest and compression damage is worst.

CPGA treats them as evidence. Motion vectors guide aggregation across frames and residuals guide aggregation within a frame, and the work introduces VCP, a dataset of 300 videos with bitstream-derived coding priors. On 18 standard sequences under low-delay B at QP=37 it gains 0.03 dB over STDR and 0.08 dB over RFDA.
What the codec already computed

Inter-frame prediction is the reason video compression works. For each block the encoder searches a reference frame for a similar block, stores the displacement as a motion vector, and encodes the difference — the residual — which is usually small and therefore cheap.

Two useful facts fall out of that search. The motion vector is an estimate of where the corresponding content sits, computed at encode time with full access to the original frames. The residual is a map of where prediction failed, which correlates strongly with edges, texture and occlusion.

Both are cheaper and cleaner than anything an enhancement network would recompute from decoded pixels. The motion estimate was made before compression damage existed, and the residual is a direct measurement of unpredictability rather than a learned guess at it.
Two aggregations, two kinds of evidence

Temporal aggregation needs to know which neighbouring frame content actually aligns with the current one. Using the codec’s motion vectors instead of re-estimating alignment removes a specific failure mode: at low bitrates the network’s own flow estimate is computed from the artifacts it is trying to remove.

Spatial aggregation needs to know where to look for repeated structure. Residuals supply that: high residual energy marks the places where local content is complex and where borrowing similar patches from elsewhere in the frame pays off most.

The design detail that matters is placement. Attaching the priors at the output would make them a correction; putting them inside the aggregation modules lets them decide which evidence is gathered in the first place — a different and stronger use of the same information.
What coding priors add

Evaluation uses standard compressed-video sequences under both low-delay B and random-access configurations at several quantization parameters, reporting average PSNR and SSIM alongside a temporal quality-fluctuation analysis.

The fluctuation measure is the right companion metric. Frame-wise averages hide flicker: a method can raise the mean while making per-frame quality oscillate, and viewers notice oscillation far more than a uniform small loss.

The reported margins — 0.03 dB over STDR and 0.08 dB over RFDA on 18 sequences at QP=37 — are small in absolute terms, which is expected this far along the curve. The ablations separating priors from aggregation modules are what distinguish gains from extra bitstream information from gains a larger pixel-based network could have bought.
Restoration beyond decoded pixels

The framing worth keeping is that a codec is not a black box that damages video and hands it over. It is a pipeline that already performed motion estimation and a prediction/decision split, and that work is reusable evidence for reconstruction.

The practical constraint is access. Motion vectors and residuals come from the bitstream; a service receiving only decoded RGB frames cannot compute them, and the same architecture should not be assumed to keep its advantage in that setting.

That makes this as much a systems paper as a model paper. The question it raises for anyone building an enhancement pipeline is where to attach the enhancer to the decoder — and the answer determines whether the reported margin is available at all.
keypoints: A codec already computes motion and separates predicted content from residual detail. CPGA reuses both: motion vectors guide temporal aggregation, residuals guide multi-scale non-local spatial aggregation.
The priors are used inside aggregation rather than appended at the output, so they decide which evidence gets gathered instead of only correcting the result afterwards.
VCP: 300 videos with bitstream-derived coding priors. On 18 standard sequences under low-delay B at QP=37, average PSNR gain is 0.03 dB over STDR and 0.08 dB over RFDA.

xpsr.headline: Using language to guide faithful super-resolution
xpsr.dek: A caption tells the diffusion model what the scene contains. It also carries the degradation that produced it — both have to be handled.
sections: Introduction

Diffusion-based super-resolution leans on a text-to-image prior to fill in what the low-resolution input lost. That prior is powerful and indifferent: given a badly degraded patch it supplies the most likely structure, which may have nothing to do with what was actually there.

Language is the obvious additional condition. A caption can say the image contains a shop sign with specific letterforms, supplying high-level context that no amount of upsampling will recover from the pixels. The difficulty is that the caption must be produced from the degraded image and therefore carries its degradation with it.

XPSR is built around that tension. It uses multimodal language models for semantic conditions, fuses them with image features through Semantic-Fusion Attention, and adds a Degradation-Free Constraint so the fused representation keeps the content without importing the corruption. On DIV2K-val it gains 10.34% in MANIQA over SeeSR.
The condition is also a carrier

A semantic condition is attractive because it operates at a level pixels cannot. At 4× or 8× downscaling with compression on top, the identity of an object can be genuinely ambiguous from the image alone, and a caption can commit to one interpretation.

But the caption is generated from the same degraded input. Compression blocks, noise and blur are all present in the encoder’s input, so whatever semantic embedding comes out has been computed over corrupted evidence — the condition is informative and contaminated at once.

Concatenating it with image features therefore does two things at once: it adds high-level guidance and it opens a second path for the degradation to reach the generative process. Any method using language this way has to separate those effects before it can claim the guidance helped.
Fusion, and a constraint on what is carried

Semantic-Fusion Attention is the mechanism for combining the two modalities. Rather than treating the caption as a fixed prefix, it lets image and semantic features interact, so the influence of language is modulated by what the image actually supports.

The Degradation-Free Constraint is the counterpart that does the separating. It pushes the fused representation toward preserving useful content while discouraging it from encoding the low-resolution image’s degradation — in effect asking the condition to describe the scene and not the damage.

The pairing is the point. Fusion alone would let a contaminated semantic signal through more effectively; the constraint alone would suppress signal along with corruption. Treating semantic assistance and degradation suppression as complementary requirements is what makes the conditioning usable.
Measuring guidance and fidelity separately

The evaluation covers synthetic degradations and real photographs, with captions produced from the degraded inputs rather than from clean references — the realistic setting, and the one that makes the constraint necessary rather than optional.

On DIV2K-val the reported relative gains over SeeSR are 10.34% in MANIQA, 8.57% in CLIPIQA and 1.64% in MUSIQ, and a real-image user study gives XPSR 64.3% of selections among six methods. These are perceptual measures, and the paper is careful to note that diffusion methods can still trail GAN-based ones on PSNR and SSIM.

That gap is not a footnote. Pixel-level similarity and perceptual quality genuinely disagree for generative restoration, and the paper treats the disagreement as a finding rather than averaging it away — a model can be preferred by humans and farther from the reference at the same time.
Semantic help without semantic invention

The conditional reading is the honest one. Better conditioning improves this pipeline under these settings; it does not establish that language can recover information absent from an image with certainty, because the caption is itself an inference from degraded evidence.

The failure mode to watch is confident misdescription. If the language model commits to the wrong object, the generative prior will render it convincingly — stronger semantic guidance raises both the quality of correct guesses and the plausibility of wrong ones.

That suggests an asymmetric deployment pattern. Use semantic conditioning where the scene is ambiguous and the interpretation is cheap to verify, and stay sceptical where a wrong guess downstream is expensive. The constraint reduces leakage; it cannot audit the caption.
keypoints: Semantic conditions come from a multimodal language model reading the degraded input, so the useful part — what the scene contains — arrives mixed with the degradation that produced it.

Semantic-Fusion Attention controls how language and image features interact, and a Degradation-Free Constraint pushes the representation to keep content without carrying the low-resolution image’s corruption into generation.

Relative gains over SeeSR on DIV2K-val: 10.34% MANIQA, 8.57% CLIPIQA, 1.64% MUSIQ, with 64.3% selection in a real-image user study — while diffusion methods still trail GAN-based ones on PSNR and SSIM.

ptmvqa.headline: Learning video quality from diverse pretrained models
ptmvqa.dek: Quality labels are scarce; pretrained representations are not. The problem is making several frozen feature spaces agree on what quality means.
sections: Introduction

Predicting how a viewer will rate a video requires knowing about its content, its distortions and its motion, and the ground truth is expensive. Subjective scores have to be collected from people one clip at a time, so quality datasets are small by the standards of modern vision.

The obvious workaround is transfer, and the usual version of transfer — fine-tuning one large pretrained backbone — borrows from a single source. Different backbones know different things: objects, motion, texture statistics. None of them was trained to judge quality.

PTM-VQA asks whether those complementary representations can be combined into one quality-aware space without fine-tuning any of them. On LSVQ-Test the reported configuration reaches PLCC 0.8637 and SRCC 0.8545, and the backbones are selected by how well their features cluster quality annotations.
Several frozen backbones, one space

Each pretrained model contributes features extracted with its weights frozen — no fine-tuning, no quality labels flowing back into the backbones. That keeps the method cheap and the pretrained knowledge intact, but the representations arrive in incompatible spaces with no shared notion of quality.

Concatenating them would not fix that. Two backbones can emit feature vectors of the same length that order clips completely differently, and a predictor trained on the concatenation has to learn the correspondence from a small quality dataset — precisely the scarce resource the method was meant to avoid depending on.

Model selection is therefore part of the method rather than a preliminary step. Candidates are ranked by clustering performance on quality-assessment data, which selects for backbones whose representations already separate quality levels instead of assuming that more sources are always better.
Consistency and separation

Two objectives shape the shared space, and they pull in different directions on purpose. Intra-consistency brings representations of the same video — however many backbones produced them — into agreement, so the space has a coherent notion of a single clip.

Inter-divisibility then separates the groups formed from the quality annotations, so similarly rated clips land near each other and differently rated clips do not. Consistency alone would collapse everything toward one point; separation alone would have nothing coherent to arrange.

The pairing is what makes the space quality-aware rather than merely aligned. Alignment is unsupervised and can be achieved with no label at all; the separation term is where subjective scores actually enter, and it is what turns a fused feature into a usable predictor.
What the constraints produce

Experiments compare pretrained feature combinations on KoNViD-1k, LIVE-VQC and YouTube-UGC, then test larger-scale training on LSVQ, with cross-database evaluation measuring transfer when nothing is fine-tuned on the target set.

Cross-database testing is the demanding condition. Within-database splits share capture conditions, content pools and distortion types with the training data; transferring between databases shares none of that, so a drop there is the honest measure of whether the space generalises or has memorised one dataset’s statistics.

PLCC and SRCC measure agreement with human judgement, and ablations examine both constraints and the clustering choices. Runtime changes with the selected backbones, so efficiency is reported for the actual combination used rather than for one default — a necessary caveat when a method’s cost depends on its configuration.
Predicting quality is a distinct task

The value of the framework is reuse: knowledge acquired for object recognition, action recognition or self-supervised video modelling is repurposed for a task that has almost no labelled data of its own.

Its output should not be over-read. A quality score is a prediction of perceived quality, not a guarantee about factual content or temporal correctness — a video can be rated highly while containing the wrong content or an impossible motion.

In a restoration system that makes VQA useful in one specific way and not another. It supports comparison and selection: choosing among candidate reconstructions, monitoring a pipeline. But a high predicted score still needs to be paired with fidelity checks and task-specific measures before it means the video is correct.
keypoints: Features come from multiple frozen pretrained models chosen by how well their representations cluster quality-annotated data — the bet is complementarity, and adding every available backbone is explicitly not assumed to help.

Two constraints shape the space: intra-consistency aligns representations of the same video, and inter-divisibility separates groups formed from the quality annotations, so the space is both coherent and predictive.

PLCC 0.8637 and SRCC 0.8545 on LSVQ-Test, with cross-database tests measuring transfer without fine-tuning on the target set — the output is a quality prediction, not a restoration or a factual claim about content.

cassr.headline: A clearer reference for generative super-resolution
cassr.dek: One diffusion pass has to infer content and generate detail at once. CasSR spends a stage on the condition first.
sections: Introduction

Real-world super-resolution asks a diffusion model to do two jobs at once. It must infer what the degraded image contains, and it must generate a high-resolution version of it — and it does both from one conditioning signal that is itself damaged.

The failure follows directly. When the condition is uninformative, the prior takes over and produces the most plausible content rather than the correct content. That is where semantic loss and invented detail come from: not from a weak prior, but from a prior asked to resolve an ambiguity it was given no evidence to resolve.

CasSR separates the two jobs in sequence. A first stage produces a preliminary reference image that is cleaner and more informative than the original observation; a second, cascaded controllable diffusion stage generates the final result from it. On DIV2K validation this improves MUSIQ by 3.82% and MANIQA by 7.05% over the next-best compared method.
Improving the evidence before generating

The first stage exists to change what the second stage receives. Rather than conditioning generation on the raw degraded observation, the cascade produces a preliminary reference — less degraded, with clearer content — and conditions the generative pass on that.

The reference is not treated as ground truth, and the distinction matters. It is better-conditioned evidence: easier to extract semantics from, closer to the clean image in the ways that guide generation, yet still a reconstruction carrying its own errors.

This is worth separating from ordinary multi-stage super-resolution. The goal of the first stage is not to produce a good image; it is to produce a condition the generative prior can use well. Those are different objectives, and judging the intermediate output as a final result misreads the design.
Keeping generation tied to the original

A cleaner reference creates its own risk: the generative stage may drift toward the reference’s interpretation and away from the actual observation. The multi-attention mechanism is the counterweight, strengthening how the text-to-image backbone draws on the original image rather than only on the reference.

This is why both stages have to be judged together. The first changes the evidence; the second decides how much that evidence is trusted versus how much the pretrained visual prior is allowed to fill in. Improving either one alone is not the same as improving the pair.

The general pattern — restore the condition, then generate — is the transferable part. Asking a powerful prior to resolve every ambiguity at once wastes its capacity; handing it a partially disambiguated input lets the same prior spend that capacity on detail.
Where the cascade preserves detail

The comparison covers GAN-based and diffusion-based methods on DIV2K validation, DRealSR and RealSR, reporting reference-based perceptual distances alongside no-reference quality measures and detailed visual comparisons.

The reported relative improvements on DIV2K validation are 3.82% in MUSIQ and 7.05% in MANIQA over the next-best compared method. Visual examples are the more informative evidence here: cases where the cascade preserves a small identifying detail — a penguin’s eye, the boundary of a wing — are exactly the cases where a single-stage prior would have substituted a plausible one.

Performance varies across DRealSR and RealSR, and that variation should be read rather than averaged. The mechanism depends on the first stage extracting usable content, so the benefit is largest where degradation is severe but structure survives, and smaller where the input is already near the limit of what the reference stage can recover.
A prior needs an anchor

The idea that generalises is making the condition an object of restoration instead of a fixed input. Most work treats conditioning as given and improves the generator; this treats the quality of the evidence as a variable worth spending a stage on.

The obvious cost is error propagation. If the preliminary stage commits to the wrong content, the second stage renders that commitment convincingly — a harder failure to detect than a one-stage hallucination, because the output looks clean and internally coherent.

That suggests how to read results of this kind. Judge a final image on attractive detail and on consistency with the original observation, and treat the two as separate checks. A cascade improving both is doing what the design claims; one improving only the first is amplifying its own errors.
keypoints: Two jobs, one condition: inferring content and generating detail are forced into a single diffusion pass, and when the condition is badly degraded the prior resolves the ambiguity by inventing.

A preliminary reference image is generated first to extract content and reduce degradation, then a cascaded controllable diffusion model generates from that reference, with a multi-attention mechanism tying the backbone back to the original image.

Relative improvements of 3.82% in MUSIQ and 7.05% in MANIQA on DIV2K validation over the next-best compared method, with visual comparisons showing retention of small identifying details such as a penguin’s eye and wing boundaries.

magvortex.headline: How vortices change the splitting of magnetic tubes
magvortex.dek: A curved magnetic tube splits itself through the dipole it induces. An accompanying vortex can stop that from happening.
sections: Introduction

A curved magnetic flux tube in a conducting fluid does not simply stay as it is. The Lorentz force acting on curved field generates a counter-rotating vortex dipole, and that dipole can tear the tube into smaller structures — a mechanism relevant wherever magnetic structures fragment and release energy.

The clean version of this problem is a magnetic tube alone. Real flows are rarely clean: a magnetic structure in a turbulent conducting fluid sits alongside vortical structures, and the two interact through the same velocity field. Whether the splitting mechanism survives that company is a separate question.

This study asks it with direct numerical simulations of linked magnetic and vortex tubes, varying their initial relative angle from zero to 45 degrees. The answer is conditional and interesting: a sufficiently strong accompanying vortex tube disrupts dipole formation and inhibits splitting.
A frame that follows the field line

The Frenet–Serret frame attaches a tangent, normal and binormal direction to every point of a curve. Applied to a magnetic field line it converts the geometry of that line — its curvature and torsion — into local coordinates for whatever force acts on it.

This matters because the Lorentz force depends on the field’s own geometry. Curvature determines the direction and magnitude of the magnetic tension force, so expressing the dynamics in the field’s own frame makes the force decomposition readable instead of leaving it buried in components.

In that description the vortex dipole is not a separate observation to be correlated with splitting after the fact. It is the flow response to the tension force, and therefore part of the mechanism — which is why anything that alters the local rotational flow should change whether splitting happens at all.
Varying the configuration

The simulations combine an analytical force decomposition with direct numerical simulation of linked magnetic and vortex tubes, varying the initial relative angle from zero to 45 degrees. Field-line geometry, vorticity generation and magnetic-to-kinetic energy transfer are examined together.

Sweeping the angle is the right control because it separates the two structures without changing either one. At zero the tubes are aligned and the vortex sits where the dipole wants to form; as the angle grows, the imposed rotation is progressively misaligned with the self-induced one.

Comparing an isolated magnetic structure with an accompanied one is the other necessary contrast. Without the isolated case you could not tell whether a change in splitting came from the vortex or merely from two structures in a periodic domain evolving differently from one.
When the vortex wins

The isolated magnetic tube behaves as expected. Curvature drives a Lorentz force, the force drives a dipole, and the dipole splits the tube into smaller structures while magnetic energy is converted into kinetic energy.

With a sufficiently strong accompanying vortex tube the outcome changes. The imposed rotational flow disrupts dipole formation before it can organise, and splitting is inhibited rather than merely delayed — the mechanism is interrupted upstream of the step that produces it.

The simulations also show sensitivity to small changes in angular configuration, and that sensitivity is worth reading carefully. A mechanism that depends on how two structures are oriented is one whose outcome in a turbulent flow cannot be predicted from local geometry alone.
From local forces to structural evolution

The result connects a local geometric description — curvature, torsion and the forces they generate — to a visible change in topology and energy release. That chain is the useful part: it explains why a tube splits rather than only recording that it did.
